title: The same certificate bound holds for degree-two functions on perfect matchings
source_title: Uniqueness for 2-Intersecting Families of Permutations and Perfect Matchings

standard_prerequisites.name: Degree of a Boolean function on matchings
standard_prerequisites.statement: The degree of f as a multilinear polynomial in the variables recording which pairs occur in the matching.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the hypothesis bounded by two.

standard_prerequisites.name: Certificate of a matching
standard_prerequisites.statement: A set of pairs prescribed to occur, whose size is the quantity bounded.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the quantity bounded by n minus two.

standard_prerequisites.name: Four-bit reduction
standard_prerequisites.statement: A certificate of size n minus one leaves just enough room to read off a four-bit function by choosing four independent alternatives in the matching.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the construction that produces the contradiction.

core_obligations: Assume the contrary, so that a degree-two function on perfect matchings has a certificate of size n minus one (source line 494).
From that certificate build a four-bit function by evaluating f on the matchings obtained by swapping four independent pairs, and transport the degree bound to it (source lines 496-497).
Conclude as in the permutation case: the transported function has degree at most two and sensitivity four, which the finite inspection excludes (source line 497).

proof_roadmap.step: Build the four-bit function from four independent pair swaps and reach the contradiction.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the author's labelled lemma at source lines 490-492, the matching analogue of the permutation bound: for n at least eight, a function on perfect matchings of degree at most two has a common certificate of size at most n minus two. The proof (source lines 493-497) repeats the shape of the permutation case in the matching language: a supposed certificate of size n minus one leaves four independent alternatives, the values of f on the matchings obtained by choosing among them give a four-bit function, and the degree bound is carried over to it so that the same finite exclusion applies. The statement records the bound and neither the reduction nor the exclusion.
